doc.title: Milt Hinton interviewed by Joe Williams, Majesty of the Seas, May 31, 1995

title: Working for Eddie South and the gangster-run clubs
summary: Hinton recalls playing with Eddie South in Al Capone's clubs, and white bandleaders coming to hear them.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: He’d mention things about Jimmy Noone. And I remember because in the 30s I remember I was working with Eddie South, a great violin player, and I got the job to play with Eddie and he had just come back from Europe. And we got to give the men or what we call on the other side the gangsters a lot of credit for helping music along, because they almost closed and they kept music. Capone’s. Al Capone had the Cotton Club on Cicero. And he had people, he opened the Cotton Club with black entertainers and white customers, and the gangsters. And he opened a club downtown, it was called the Club

Rubaiyat, for his gangster pals just to have some place to come and bring their ladies to have lunch. It seated like 75 or 100 people. He put Eddie South in there. And we played all these different places for him. And I remember, Dix Debill was the conductor for Ben Bernie’s band. And his father was a violin player. So he used to bring his father over to hear Eddie South. And Ben Pollock was playing a club in Chicago. And Jack Teagarden, Benny Goodman —
Woody Herman, all that bunch came out through Ben Pollock.
That’s right. They would come over and hang out with us on the other side.
